comment.text:
3-Dehydroquinate dehydratase (DHQ dehydratase) is involved in the 3rd step of the chorismate pathway, which leads to the biosynthesis of aromatic amino acids. DHQ dehydratase catalyzes the conversion of DHQ to 3-dehydroshikimate and introduces the first double bond of the aromatic ring [Mitsuhashi54]. 

The first step of the 3-dehydroquinase reaction involves the formation of an imine intermediate between the keto group of 3-dehydroquinate and the e-amino group of a lysine at the active site of the enzyme. Chemical modification and mutagenesis experiments have identified this lysine to be Lys-170 [Chaudhuri91]. In addition to the lysine side chain involved in imine formation, the enzyme also requires a basic group for proton abstraction. His-143 has been shown to be essential for catalysis in this enzyme and that this residue may be acting as the general base in the catalytic mechanism. His-143 may also be involved in Schiff base formation/breakdown. [Leech95]

The pH activity studies demonstrate that 3-dehydroquinase requires groups with pKa values near 6 in a deprotonated form for maximal activity. Experiments with diethylpyrocarbonate provide evidence that this group is the imidazole side chain of a histidine residue. [Chaudhuri86] The reaction exhibits cis stereochemistry in both directions [Mitsuhashi54].

The structural gene, aroD, has been cloned and overexpressed [Duncan86a]. Crystals of DHQ dehydratase in E. coli and Salmonella typhi were grown. However, only the S. typhi DHQ dehydratase structure has been resolved to 2.3 Å resolution. The E. coli and S. typhi DHQ dehydratase is 69% identical at the amino acid level [Servos91].

DHQ-SDH is a multifunctional enzyme.
The enzyme atalyzes two consecutive reactions in the shikimate biosynthesis pathway, transforming 3-dehydroquinate (DQ) to 3-dehydroshikimate (DHS) and then to shikimate [Singh06].

In addition, the enzyme can catalyze the oxidation of 3-dehydroshikimate to 3,5-didehydroshikimate, which immidiately and spontaneously rearranges to form gallate [Muir11a].

The enzyme has been co-crystalized with a few different substrates to elucidate its structure and bifunctional behavior  [Singh06, Singh07]. These studies reveal that the enzyme has a concave architecture that places the active sites for the two different enzymatic activities in a face-to-face arrangement. Two compounds associated with the first reaction DQ and DHS can be siphoned off into quinate metabolic pathways. While quinates may act as important anti-herbivory and cell wall precursor compounds, it is likley important for plants to maintain a constant flux through the shikimate pathway. The bifunctional nature of this enzyme may promote that outcome by creating a higher effective concentration of DHS at the shikimate dehydrogenase active site, thus reducing the tendency for DHS to exit the chorismate biosynthetic pathway [Singh06]. A series of single amino-acid change shikimate dehydrogenase active site mutants were tested in vitro to better understand this phenomenon [Singh06, Singh07]. The dehydroquinate dehydratase activity was not extensively characterized, but, when DQ was added to the DHQ-SDH crystal, it led to the formation of a Lys-241-dehydroshikimate Schiff base in the dehydroquinate dehydratase active site [Singh07].

This protein is localized to the cholorplast [Rutschow08] and may be present in the stroma [Zybailov08]. Studies on DHQ-SDH were performed using a truncated version of the protein lacking the first 88-amino acids of the full-length protein. They are predicted to serve as the N-terminal transit peptide directing this protein to the chloroplast [Singh06, Singh07].

The asbF gene of Bacillus anthracis Sterne was cloned and expressed  in Escherichia coli in two forms - one with a His6 tag fused to the N terminus, and a second with a cleavable tag fused to the C terminus. The proteins were purified, and used for in vitro biochemical analysis and for crystallization [Pfleger08].

The enzyme is dimeric, and has a requirement for divalent ions, with a preference for Mn2+. It's structure adopts a TIM barrel cofiguration, with the N terminus burried at the bottom part of the barrel [Pfleger08].

A homologous protein has been purified from Bacillus thuringiensis [] serovar konkukian str. 97-27 [Fox08a].

The protein provides an attractive drug target.

Two types of 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase enzymes are known. The type I enzymes (encoded by genes similar to aroD) have been found to participate only in the biosynthetic shikimate pathway, which forms chorismate (see chorismate biosynthesis I and superpathway of chorismate metabolism). Type II enzymes can participate either in the biosynthetic pathway or in the catabolic quinate degradation pathway [Kleanthous92].

This type II enzyme from Amycolatopsis methanolica is unusual, since it participates in both the catabolic and the biosynthetic pathways [Euverink92]. The enzyme was purified over 1700-fold to homogeneity from its native host, and found to form a dodecameric structure. The 3-dehydroshikimate produced by the enzyme was shown to be partly used for the biosynthesis of aromatic amino acids, and partly catabolized via protocatechuate and the beta-ketoadipate pathway [Euverink92].

Corynebacterium glutamicum grows well with either L-quinate or shikimate as the sole carbon source [Teramoto09]. 
Disruption of qsuD, which encodes quinate/shikimate dehydrogenase, completely suppressed growth with either of these substrates but did not affect growth with glucose, indicating that the enzyme participates in the catabolism of quinate/shikimate but not in the biosynthetic shikimate pathway [Teramoto09].

Expression of the qsuD gene and the other genes in its operon is strongly induced during growth with either quinate or shikimate [Teramoto09].

The gene has been cloned and expressed in Escherichia coli and the recombinant protein was purified and characterized [Schoepe08]. The crystal structure has been sloved at 1.6 Å [Schoepe08].
The protein, which forms a homodimer in solution, has a lower Km for L-quinate than for shikimate, resulting in catalytic efficiency that is more than three times higher with the former.

The enzyme has a clear preference for NAD+ over NADP+. The turnover number decreases by more than 300-fold with NADP+ [Schoepe08].

YdiB was identified as a quinate/shikimate dehydrogenase.  The low catalytic efficiency of YdiB with both quinate and shikimate suggests that neither may be the physiological substrate [Michel03].  Wild-type E. coli is not known to synthesize quinate or to use it as a source of carbon.

Phylogenomic analysis of the shikimate dehydrogenase family showed that the two enzymes encoded in E. coli, AroE and YdiB, belong to different subclasses; the authors suggested that YdiB was acquired by horizontal gene transfer.  Common and subclass-specific catalytic residues and substrate binding motifs were identified [Singh08].  

YdiB can use both NAD+ or NADP+ as a cosubstrate for catalysis [Michel03].  Because the intracellular concentration of NAD+ is 40-fold higher than that of NADH+, the dehydrogenase direction is expected to be favored by YdiB in vivo [Johansson06].  Conversely, AroE is NADP+- and substrate-specific and has much higher catalytic efficiency than YdiB [Michel03].  aroE mutant data and the results from metabolic engineering experiments strongly suggest that YdiB is unable to replace AroE under normal physiological conditions.  Expression of YdiB for engineering of L-tyrosine production led to accumulation of the pathway intermediates dehydroquinate and dehydroshikimate and the side product quinate [Juminaga12].

Crystal structures of YdiB have been solved at 2.3 Å and 2.5 Å resolution [Benach03, Michel03]. Although AroE and YdiB have low sequence similarity, they have high structural similarity with two α/β domains separated by a wide cleft [Michel03].  Results from site-directed mutagenesis of predicted active-site residues do not support a general acid-base mechanism for catalysis [Lindner05].

Quinate is produced as a by-product in a genetically modified shikimate-producing E. coli strain [Draths99, Knop01] and can be attributed to YdiB activity [Garcia17a].  Expression of ydiB in a shikimate-producing strain is only induced under carbon-limiting growth conditions [Johansson06].

comment.text:
Two types of 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase enzymes are known. The type I enzymes (encoded by genes similar to aroD) have been found to participate only in the biosynthetic shikimate pathway, which forms chorismate (see chorismate biosynthesis I and superpathway of chorismate metabolism). Type II enzymes can participate either in the biosynthetic pathway or in the catabolic quinate degradation pathway [Kleanthous92].

The bacterium Gluconobacter oxydans possesses two dehydroquinate dehydratase enzymes - a soluble cytoplasmic biosynthetic enzyme and a membrane-bound periplasmic catabolic enzyme. Both enzymes were purified and found to have similar catalytic properties [Adachi08].

The periplasmic enzyme, like many other type II enzymes, forms a homododecamer complex.

Methanococcus maripaludis is a strictly anaerobic, methane-producing archaeon.
This organism can synthesize aromatic amino acids by a de novo pathway, with chorismate as an intermediate.
3-dehydroquinate dehydratase activity, the third step in the de novo pathway, has been measured in cell-free extracts
and found to be 6.0 +/- 0.2 mU/mg [Porat04].

aroD, the gene that encodes the enzyme, has been deleted [Porat04]. This mutant required
all three AroAAs for growth, and no DHQ activity was detectible in cell extracts.

3-dehydroshikimate dehydratase catalyzes the dehydration of 3-dehydroshikimate to protocatechuate. 
The Neurospora crassa enzyme has been purified 1650-fold to homogeneity and found to be a monomeric protein of 37 kDa [Stroman78].

The purified enzyme was extremely sensitive to thermal denaturation, but was significantly stabilized by Mg2+ ions. In addition, maximal catalytic activity required the presence of a divalent cation, including Mg2+, Mo2+, Mn2+, Ba2+ and Co2+ [Stroman78].

The qa-4, which encodes the enzyme, has been isolated and sequenced [Rutledge84].

The qutB gene, encoding the quinate dehydrogenase of Aspergillus nidulans, has been cloned by PCR and expressed in Escherichia coli as a GST-fusion protein.
The recombinant protein, which was able to complement an aroE mutation in the Escherichia coli host, was purified to homogeneity and found to be a monomeric protein [Hawkins93a]. The protein could accept shikimate as well, but the Km for this substrate was more than three fold higher than that for L-quinate.

The product of the qsuB gene of Corynebacterium glutamicum R has not been characterized. However, there are several reason to assume that it encodes dehydroshikimate dehydratase. First, the gene is present in an operon with other genes involved in the degradation of L-quinate and shikimate. Secondly, the amino-terminal half of the QsuB protein has 25% amino acid sequence identity to dehydroshikimate dehydratases identified in fungi, and thridly, the gene expression is induced during growth on L-quinate or shikimate.
Curiously, the caroxy-terminal half of the enzyme has 25% amino acid sequence identity to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase [Teramoto09].

The product of the qsuC gene of Corynebacterium glutamicum R has not been characterized. However, there are several reason to assume that it encodes 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase. First, the gene is present in an operon with other genes involved in the degradation of L-quinate and shikimate. Secondly, the amino acid sequence of this protein has 60% identity to type II dehydroquinate dehydratase from Streptomyces coelicolor, and thridly, the gene expression is induced during growth on L-quinate or shikimate [Teramoto09].

Two types of 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase enzymes are known. The type I enzymes (encoded by genes similar to aroD) have been found to participate only in the biosynthetic shikimate pathway, which forms chorismate (see chorismate biosynthesis I and superpathway of chorismate metabolism). Type II enzymes can participate either in the biosynthetic pathway or in the catabolic quinate degradation pathway [Kleanthous92].

The Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 quiB gene, which encodes a catabolic 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase, is an oddity, since depite being involved in a catabolic pathway, it bears closest resemblance (41.9% identity) to the aroD gene of E. faecalis, which is a type I enzyme [Elsemore95]. The evolution of quiB towards a catabolic role appears to have been accompanied by fusion of a leader sequence for transport of the protein into the inner membrane.

The quiC gene of Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 was found following the quiB gene within a single operon, which also contains the quiX gene. The quiC gene was cloned and sequenced, and had no close matches to sequences available at the time [Elsemore95]. The gene is not common, and has only been found in members of the Acinetobacter genus and potentially a few strains of Pseudomonas putida.

The Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 gene was expressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant cells had a specific 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase activity of 19.5 mmol/min/mg of protein [Elsemore95].

General Background

L-quinate is a naturally occuring compound found in decaying plant matter [Hawkins93].
Quinate is one of several aromatic compounds that can be metabolized by microorganisms to the
central intermediate protocatechuate that can be further metabolized via the β-ketoadipate pathway to acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA [Tresguerres70, Adachi03a]. Bacteria capable of using quinate as a sole carbon source were observed as early as 1911 [Beijerinck11]

Quinate degradation was initially studied in the fungus Neurospora crassa [Tatum54], and later in other fungi (such as Aspergillus nidulans [Hawkins85]) and bacteria, including Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 (at the time reported as Acinetobacter calcoaceticus) [Elsemore95, Elsemore94], Gluconobacter oxydans [Adachi03a] and Corynebacterium glutamicum [Schoepe08].| Many of these organisms can grow on quinate as a sole carbon and energy source, and the pathway is inducible by growth on either L-quinate, shikimate, or protocatechuate.

Two variants of this pathway are present in MetaCyc; the main difference between them lies in the enzyme that catalyzes the initial oxidation of L-quinate. Filamentous fungi and Gram-positive bacteria use an NAD(P)-dependent enzyme (EC 1.1.1.24), while Gram-negative bacteria use a pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)-dependent enzyme (EC 1.1.99.25) [vanKleef88]. The later pathway is desribed in quinate degradation I.

About This Pathway

Quinate degradation was first studied in filamentous fungi such as Neurospora crassa and Aspergillus nidulans. The fungal pathway starts with conversion of L-quinate to 3-dehydroquinate by an NAD-dependent quinate/shikimate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.24). The genes involved in the fungal pathway  (qa genes in Neurospora crassa, qut genes in Aspergillus nidulans ) were shown to be present in a single cluster, and are induced by growth on either L-quinate or shikimate [Patel81, Wheeler96, Hawkins93]. The clusters include a gene encoding a permease that enables L-quinate to enter the organism [Whittington87].

An NAD-dependent enzyme is also present in certain Gram-positive bacteria, such as Corynebacterium glutamicum [Teramoto09]. As in the fungi, the qsuD gene, which encodes the Corynebacterium glutamicum enzyme, is located in a gene cluster that also contains the genes encoding the rest of the pathway's enzymes. The cluster, which is under the control of the QsuR regulator, is induced by growth on L-quinate shikimate [Teramoto09].

The the pentafunctional AROM polypeptide of Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a large polypeptide that represents the fusion of five different genes. The enzymes catalyzes five different reactions in the shikimate pathway, and is a mosaic of five monofunctional domains [Duncan87].

The ARO1 gene has been cloned and sequenced [Duncan87].
Expression of a cloned  ARO1 gene was shown to be regulated in response to amino acid limitation by the well characterised S. cerevisiae 'general control' mechanism [Duncan88].

The Saccharomyces cerevisiae enzyme has not been purified, but a similar enzyme from Neurospora crassa has been purified and investigated [Coggins87].
